paras: The attempted lynching of Hugh Armstead took place on the evening of November 3, 1903, election day, in Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, when a crowd of 500 or more men chased Armstead, a Black man, to the Monongahela River crying "Lynch him" after he shot Patrick Butler, a watcher at the polls. Police fought the crowd for their prisoner and took him safely to jail. A single Associated Press dispatch about the case ran in papers across the country, in some of them among reports of election-day violence elsewhere, and the Richmond Planet reprinted it.

Butler was a watcher at the polls in the jail voting precinct, and the dispatch stated that the shooting "had no connection with politics." In Butler's account, he and several companions were playfully contesting for possession of his cane, and Armstead was struck by it as he passed. Butler said Armstead then drew a revolver and fired "without other provocation," and other unnamed witnesses said Armstead had no provocation whatever. Armstead said instead that one of the crowd had hit him in the mouth with his fist and that he shot in return.

The bullet pierced Butler's liver, and physicians said he could not recover. Armstead ran along Ross Street, Fifth Avenue and Smithfield Street to the Monongahela River, followed by an "excited crowd of 500 or more men" who kept up "a continual cry of 'Lynch him.'" When he was finally captured, the police "had a desperate fight with the crowd to protect their prisoner." They got him into an engine house and later took him to jail.

The coverage gives no account of arrests among the crowd, of Butler's death, or of an inquest or trial of Armstead. Weekly news digests nonetheless called Armstead "the colored murderer of Patrick Butler."

The story reached readers as a single wire dispatch, credited by the Raleigh News & Observer to the Associated Press, and appeared in morning papers on November 4 from Washington and New Haven to St. Louis, Omaha, Montgomery, Birmingham and Savannah. The Evening Star headed it "Attempt to Lynch Negro" and the St. Louis Republic "Lynching Barely Averted," while the Omaha Daily Bee printed it as "Lynching at Pittsburg Averted" in a column of election-day shootings that also reported a lynching at Lake Village, Arkansas. Several shortened versions, among them those of the St. Louis Republic, the Savannah Morning News and the Raleigh paper, left out Armstead's account of being struck and gave only Butler's.

Some Southern papers put the shooting ahead of the mob in their headlines: "Negro Angers Crowd" in the Montgomery Advertiser and "Negro Fatally Wounds an Election Watcher" in the Birmingham Age-Herald. Five days later the Atlanta Constitution ran the dispatch as "Quakers Hot After Negro," casting the would-be lynchers as Pennsylvanians. A syndicated version datelined November 4 carried the subhead "Pittsburg Negro Shot Watcher at Polls Without Provocation" in the Milford Chronicle and the Fredericksburg Free Lance. One-line digests in small weeklies, and a Czech-language summary in Pokrok západu, carried the story into mid-November.

The only Black-press account found was in the Richmond Planet of November 7, which printed the full syndicated text, including its "Without Provocation" headline, in a front-page column otherwise given to a Knights of Pythias carnival. The Planet added no comment of its own, but its text kept Armstead's statement that he had been struck in the mouth before he fired.

What led to the shooting rests on conflicting accounts in the same dispatch: Butler and other witnesses said Armstead was touched by a cane in horseplay and fired without provocation, while Armstead said he was punched in the mouth first. The Omaha Daily Bee datelined the dispatch November 2 and the syndicated version November 4, but most printings, under a November 3 dateline, placed the events on "this evening," election day.
